name: Arjuna Visada Yoga
subtitle: The Yoga of Arjuna's Despair
summary: On the eve of the great war, the blind king Dhritarashtra asks his charioteer Sanjaya what is happening at Kurukshetra. The armies are counted, the conches roar, and Arjuna asks Krishna to drive his chariot between the two sides. Seeing teachers, cousins and friends ready to die, the greatest archer of his age lays down his bow. Every journey into wisdom begins with an honest crisis.

sections.label: The Armies
sections.title: Two armies, one question
sections.intro: The blind king can't see the field, so he asks. Duryodhana, anxious beneath his confidence, names warrior after warrior on both sides.
sections.gyan: Before you build anything, survey the field honestly: what you have, what you lack, and why you're really doing it.

sections.label: The Conches
sections.title: The conches roar
sections.intro: Bhishma blows his conch and the whole battlefield answers. Krishna's Panchajanya and Arjuna's Devadatta ring out, each one named, and the sound shakes the hearts of the Kauravas.
sections.gyan: Every great undertaking has a moment when you commit out loud. After that, there's no pretending it isn't happening.

sections.label: The Chariot
sections.title: Between the two armies
sections.intro: Arjuna, his banner bearing Hanuman, asks Krishna to place the chariot in the middle. Krishna does, and simply says: look.
sections.gyan: Sometimes the most useful thing a mentor can do is put you where you can see clearly, and then stay quiet.

sections.label: Arjuna's Despair
sections.title: The bow falls
sections.intro: Facing his own family, Arjuna's body fails him and his reasoning spirals: kinship, sin, tradition, ruin. He sits down, lets the Gandiva fall to the ground, and weeps. Krishna has not spoken yet.
sections.gyan: Breakdowns often arrive dressed as good arguments. Naming the crisis is the first step; the answer begins in Chapter 2.

name: Sankhya Yoga
subtitle: The Yoga of Knowledge
summary: Arjuna, in tears, asks to be taught. Krishna smiles and the Gita begins: the Self that is never born and never dies, the duty that is yours alone, the art of acting without clinging to results, and the portrait of a person whose wisdom stays steady. Chapter 2 holds the whole Gita in miniature.

sections.label: The Disciple
sections.title: Teach me, I take refuge in you
sections.intro: Krishna's first words are a challenge, not comfort. Arjuna argues back, then breaks open and becomes a student. "I will not fight," he says, and falls silent.
sections.gyan: Real learning starts the moment you admit you don't know. Verse 2.7 is that moment.

sections.label: The Self
sections.title: What never dies
sections.intro: Krishna begins with the eternal Self: never born, never dying, untouched by weapons, fire, water or wind. Bodies change like clothes; the one who wears them does not.
sections.gyan: Projects end, roles change, code gets rewritten. Who you are beneath the work is what lasts.

sections.label: Svadharma
sections.title: Your own duty
sections.intro: Then a practical turn: as a warrior, this fight is Arjuna's duty. Walking away would cost him his honour; meeting victory and defeat alike would free him from sin.
sections.gyan: Know your craft and own it. Equanimity isn't indifference: it's showing up the same way whether you win or lose.

sections.label: Karma Yoga
sections.title: Skill in action
sections.intro: Now the heart of it: act, but let go of the fruits. Like a tree that gives its fruit away, do the work and release the result. Evenness of mind is yoga, and yoga is skill in action. Here is the verse this whole site is built on, 2.47.
sections.gyan: Ship the work, learn, ship again. Do it well because it is yours to do, not for the metrics.

sections.label: Steady Wisdom
sections.title: The one whose mind is still
sections.intro: Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like. Krishna answers: content within, unshaken by sorrow or pleasure, and able to gather the senses in, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs.
sections.gyan: Not every notification deserves your attention. Draw the senses in, like the tortoise, and the work gets your whole mind.

sections.label: The Ocean
sections.title: Full, and still
sections.intro: Krishna traces how a mind falls (attachment, desire, anger, delusion, ruin) and how it is saved: discipline, calm, peace. The wise are like the ocean: rivers keep pouring in, and it stays full and still.
sections.gyan: Attachment, desire, anger, delusion, ruin (2.62–2.63) is a stack trace for the mind. Catch it at the first frame.

name: Karma Yoga
subtitle: The Yoga of Action
summary: Arjuna, confused, asks why he must act at all if knowledge is higher. Krishna's answer is the yoga of action: no one can stop acting, so act as an offering, keep the great wheel of the world turning, lead by example, and know the real enemy, desire, which hides wisdom the way smoke hides fire. Like the sun, the wise never stop working.

sections.label: Why Act?
sections.title: No one is ever still
sections.intro: If knowledge is higher, Arjuna asks, why push me into this terrible war? Krishna answers that no one can stay without acting even for a moment: the three qualities of nature keep everyone moving. Better to act well than to pretend to renounce.
sections.gyan: Doing nothing is not an option, only a disguise. The real choice is how you act, not whether.

sections.label: The Wheel of Yajna
sections.title: Work as an offering
sections.intro: Krishna describes the great cycle: action becomes offering, offering brings rain, rain brings grain, grain sustains beings, and beings act again (3.14). Whoever only takes from the wheel and gives nothing back, he says, is simply a thief.
sections.gyan: Everything you rely on was built by someone else's work. Give back to the wheel: docs, reviews, open source, mentoring.

sections.label: Lead by Example
sections.title: Whatever the best do, others follow
sections.intro: Even one who needs nothing should keep working for the good of the world, as King Janaka did. Krishna himself, with nothing left to gain, never stops, because if he did, everyone would follow. One lamp lights the next.
sections.gyan: People copy what you do, not what you say. If you lead, work like the standard you want the team to keep.

sections.label: The Doer
sections.title: "I am the doer"
sections.intro: Nature's qualities do the work, yet the ego wears the crown and says "I did this." Krishna asks Arjuna to offer every action to him, to watch the pull of liking and disliking, and to keep to his own dharma, even imperfectly, rather than live someone else's well.
sections.gyan: Your own path done imperfectly beats someone else's done well (3.35). Stop benchmarking against other people's lives.

sections.label: The Enemy
sections.title: Fire covered by smoke
sections.intro: What pushes people into wrong, Arjuna asks, even against their will? Desire, says Krishna, and its twin, anger. It covers wisdom as smoke covers fire, dust a mirror, the womb an unborn child. It lives in the senses, mind and intellect, but the Self is higher than all three.
sections.gyan: Senses, mind, intellect, Self (3.42): know the chain of command, and let the highest one decide.

name: Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga
meaning: Path of Knowledge and the Disciplines of Action
subtitle: The Yoga of Knowledge and Renunciation of Action
summary: Krishna reveals that this yoga is ancient, handed down from the sun, and that he himself comes into the world age after age whenever dharma falls. Then the deeper teaching: seeing inaction in action, treating every act as an offering, and the knowledge that burns karma to ash and cuts doubt like a sword.

sections.label: The Lineage
sections.title: An ancient yoga, handed down
sections.intro: This teaching is not new. Krishna gave it to the sun, the sun to Manu, Manu to King Ikshvaku. Passed from teacher to student, it was lost over time, and now he gives it again, to Arjuna, his friend.
sections.gyan: Knowledge survives only when someone passes it on. Write it down, teach it, hand it forward.

sections.label: The Avatar
sections.title: Age after age
sections.intro: How could Krishna, born so recently, have taught the ancient sun? He reveals that he has had many births, and that whenever dharma declines he comes forth, to protect the good, end wrongdoing and set dharma on its feet again (4.7–4.8).
sections.gyan: When things break down, someone has to step in. Sometimes that someone is you.

sections.label: All Paths
sections.title: However you come, I receive you
sections.intro: Whichever way people approach him, Krishna meets them there. He acts in the world yet is never stained by it, and those who understand this act freely, as the seekers of old did.
sections.gyan: There's no single right way in. Begin from where you are.

sections.label: Action in Inaction
sections.title: The still centre of the wheel
sections.intro: What is action, and what is inaction? Even sages are confused. The wise see inaction in action and action in inaction: fully engaged, yet doing nothing, because the craving for results has been burned away in the fire of knowledge.
sections.gyan: The best engineers in a crisis are the busiest and the calmest at once. Do the work fully; let the centre stay still.

sections.label: Many Offerings
sections.title: Everything is an offering
sections.intro: It opens with 4.24, recited before meals across India: the offering, the ladle, the fire and the one who offers are all Brahman. Then Krishna names the many forms of yajna: wealth, austerity, study, breath, the senses themselves. Greatest of all is the offering of knowledge.
sections.gyan: Time, attention, effort, breath: everything you put into the work is an offering. Choose where it goes.

sections.label: The Fire of Knowledge
sections.title: The boat and the sword
sections.intro: Learn from those who have seen the truth, with humility, questions and service. Knowledge is a boat across every wrong and a fire that turns action to ash. Doubt destroys, so cut it with the sword of knowledge, and stand up.
sections.gyan: Ask good questions of people who know (4.34). Then cut the doubt and get up. The answer was never to stay seated.

name: Karma Sanyasa Yoga
subtitle: The Yoga of Renunciation
summary: Arjuna asks again: renounce action, or act? Krishna says both lead to freedom, but acting without attachment is better, and in truth they are one. The one who acts this way lives in the body like a calm resident of a city of nine gates, sees all beings with an equal eye, and stays untouched, like a lotus leaf that water cannot wet.

sections.label: Two Paths
sections.title: Two rivers, one water
sections.intro: Arjuna wants one clear answer: renounce, or act? Krishna says both lead to the highest good, but acting without attachment is better, and only children call the two different. Whoever sees them as one, sees (5.5).
sections.gyan: Thinking and doing aren't rival camps. The best work has both, flowing into the same river.

sections.label: Untouched
sections.title: The city of nine gates
sections.intro: The yogi sees, hears, eats, walks and breathes, and knows it is only the senses moving among their objects. Offering everything, they stay unstained like a lotus leaf on water, and rest in the body like a calm resident of a city with nine gates.
sections.gyan: Let inputs come and go through the gates. Stay the resident, not the traffic.

sections.label: The Sun of Knowledge
sections.title: Ignorance slides away
sections.intro: The Lord does not hand out credit or blame; nature does the acting. Knowledge is only covered by ignorance, like a sun in eclipse, and when ignorance is removed, knowledge shines like the sun and lights up the Supreme.
sections.gyan: Clarity isn't added, it's uncovered. Most bugs in thinking are just something blocking the light.

sections.label: The Equal Eye
sections.title: One light on all
sections.intro: The wise see the same in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste (5.18). Unmoved by pleasant and unpleasant, they find a happiness within that outer pleasures, which begin and end, can never give.
sections.gyan: Treat the intern and the CEO with the same respect. Equal vision is wisdom, not politeness.

sections.label: The Inner Light
sections.title: Lit from within
sections.intro: Happy within, delighting within, lit from within: such a one reaches the peace of Brahman. Krishna gives a first glimpse of meditation, shutting out outer contacts, gaze between the brows, the breath made even, and the next chapter takes it further.
sections.gyan: Before a hard decision, close the tabs and even out the breath. Five quiet minutes is a real tool.

name: Dhyana Yoga
subtitle: The Yoga of Meditation
summary: Krishna turns to meditation: lift yourself by your own self, sit on a steady seat with spine straight, eat and sleep in moderation, and let the mind become like a lamp in a windless place. Arjuna objects that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees, and gives the answer: practice and detachment. And no sincere effort is ever lost.

sections.label: The Climb
sections.title: Lift yourself by yourself
sections.intro: The true renunciate is the one who does the work without leaning on its fruit. For one climbing to yoga, action is the means; for one who has arrived, calm is the means. You are your own friend and your own enemy (6.5).
sections.gyan: No one can climb for you. Be the friend who pulls you up, not the voice that drags you down.

sections.label: The Seat
sections.title: A steady seat, a straight spine
sections.intro: Krishna gives practical instructions: a clean, quiet place; a seat neither too high nor too low, of kusha grass, deerskin and cloth; body, head and neck straight; the gaze resting. And balance: neither too much food nor too little, neither too much sleep nor too little.
sections.gyan: Set up the environment and the habit wins. Sleep, food and a clean desk are part of the practice.

sections.label: The Windless Lamp
sections.title: A flame that does not flicker
sections.intro: The settled mind is like a lamp in a windless place (6.19). There, beyond the senses, is a happiness nothing can shake. And when the restless mind wanders off, simply bring it back, gently, again and again.
sections.gyan: Focus isn't never drifting. It's noticing the drift and coming back, every time (6.26).

sections.label: In All Beings
sections.title: The Self in all, all in the Self
sections.intro: The yogi sees the Self in every being and every being in the Self, like a net of jewels where each one reflects all the others. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere is never lost to him, and feels another's joy and pain as their own.
sections.gyan: Empathy is just accurate seeing: the person across the table is running on the same stuff you are.

sections.label: The Restless Mind
sections.title: As hard to hold as the wind
sections.intro: Arjuna is honest: the mind is restless, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, but it can be held, by practice (abhyasa) and detachment (vairagya), the way a string holds a kite in the wind.
sections.gyan: You won't stop the wind. Practice is the string and detachment is letting the kite fly. Hold both.

sections.label: No Effort Lost
sections.title: Nothing good is ever wasted
sections.intro: And if someone tries and falls short, do they vanish like a torn cloud? Never, says Krishna. No one who does good comes to a bad end. The practice carries over, life after life, until it reaches the goal. So be a yogi, Arjuna.
sections.gyan: Every honest attempt compounds. The practice you start today is never wasted, even if it takes far longer than you hoped.
